steps.label: Apply the property and simplify tan(π/4 − x)
steps.margin_note: First three marks — the heaviest step. Get the tan(A−B) formula exactly right before simplifying further.
steps.memory_tip: tan(π/4 − x) = (1 − tanx)/(1 + tanx) — memorise this special case of tan(A−B) with A = π/4 (tan π/4 = 1).
steps.why: The tan(A−B) formula with A = π/4 (where tan π/4 = 1) gives a clean fraction (1−tanx)/(1+tanx); adding 1 to it collapses the numerator to a plain 2, which is the key simplification the rest of the proof depends on.
common_mistakes: Using the tan(A+B) formula instead of tan(A−B).
Forgetting to combine the fraction over the common denominator (1+tanx) before adding 1.

steps.label: Substitute back and isolate I on one side
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. log(2/(1+tanx)) splits into log2 minus log(1+tanx) — the second piece is exactly I again.
steps.memory_tip: log(a/b) = log a − log b — always split a log of a fraction this way before integrating term by term.
steps.why: Splitting the log of a fraction into a difference of two logs isolates a term identical to the original I, so the equation becomes I = (a constant) − I — solvable for I by simple algebra.
common_mistakes: Not recognising that the second integral is exactly I again.
Evaluating log2 ∫dx incorrectly as log2 instead of (π/4)log2.

steps.label: Solve for I
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Add I to both sides and halve.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever I = (constant) − I appears, add I to both sides to get 2I = (constant).
steps.why: Adding I to both sides of I = (π/4)log2 − I gives 2I = (π/4)log2 directly, and dividing by 2 gives the final value.
common_mistakes: Subtracting I instead of adding it, giving 0 = (π/4)log2.
Forgetting to divide by 2 at the very last step.
